instructions:
You are reading the plain-language text of a codebase map. A reader meets each field ALONE, inside one box, with no paragraph around it, and does not read code.

Judge ONLY these two things:
  1. UNKNOWN WORD — a term the reader has not met and the field does not explain. Product words and words already in the map's Glossary are fine; jargon, an internal codename, or an unexplained abbreviation is not.
  2. LOST PRECISION — the sentence is short and plain but says nothing specific. "The system checks the user" is the shape: grammatical, readable, and it names no decision, no data and no actor. This is the worse failure, because it looks correct.

Do NOT report sentence length, em dashes, code names or an opening "It" — those are counted deterministically and the lead already has the numbers.
Be conservative. Report a field only when you can say WHICH word is unknown, or WHAT the sentence should have said. If in doubt, pass the field.

For each field you flag, return its `where` exactly as given, one of `unknown word` or `lost precision`, and one short line naming the word or the missing specific.

fields.text: Decides what counts as a claim being challenged, and what a partial pass is allowed to record.
Decides which line stands as evidence for a claim, and when a stored one has drifted.
Decides how many boxes a screen may hold, and what regrouping is allowed to change.
Decides which view a thing belongs to, and which facts a picture may leave off a box.
Decides which files a build may open, and where a change has to be written to survive.
Decides which requests the local map server answers, and which files it will hand back.
Decides whether two scores are comparable at all, and how far a measurement may move.
Someone who has cloned this project asks to install it. Their coding agent gains a new command, and the tools it drives are built and ready.
A person asks their coding agent for a map of a project that has none. A map of that project exists, pinned to the commit it describes.
A person names committed code the map is not meant to describe. Later maps leave that code out, and every count the tools print says so.
A person starts the local map server. Every project they have mapped is listed on one page in their browser.
A person opens a project's map. They see what the product does and drill from one feature down to a single box.
A reader picks the code link on a box. The file opens at that line, in their own editor or on the code host.
The code has moved on since the map was pinned. A report names the parts of the map the change touched.
A person agrees the change report is right. The map is edited to match, re-pinned, and checked again.
A person asks in plain language for a part of the map to move, split or be renamed. The map is edited in place and passes its checks.
Someone changed the instructions and wants to know the cost. Two maps of one project are scored and compared, with a verdict.
A build has finished and its chat is on disk. A report names the friction, the bugs and the gaps that run revealed.
A code link claiming an action must name the acting line, never a definition, an import or a comment.
A reader follows the link and lands on a heading instead of the work.
A decision's evidence is exactly one numbered line, or a note saying no single line enforces the decision.
Evidence naming a whole file cannot be checked, so nobody can prove the decision wrong.
Only a link claiming an action fires there is checked against the line. A link showing where a thing is defined is not.
Correct links to definitions would be reported as wrong, drowning the real findings.
A code link on the wrong line is only a warning, because the claim it carries can still be true.
A map can ship with links pointing at the wrong lines.
A stored link is judged out of date only when most reviewers agreed the claim it carries is true.
A single doubtful reading would move a link that was right all along.
A claim whose code link deliberately points at a declaration is never moved onto the line a reviewer read.
A record's link would slide off its definition onto one write line.
A corrected code link is refused when it lands in a file that neither end of the relation claims.
A link could point into a third part's code.
A person may excuse one code link a check called out. The note must quote the whole claim, then give the reason.
One short note could silence every finding about one part of the product.
Two maps are scored against each other only when both describe the same code. A run over changed code refuses.
A change in the code would read as a change in the map's quality. A scoring run must never confuse the two.
A map built over uncommitted code can never be scored, and nobody may waive that refusal.
The code such a map describes exists in no commit. Scoring it badly hands the other map a free pass on every check.
Two quality scores compare only when one judging setup produced both, so a changed setup forces a fresh judging.
Scores kept from an older judging setup read as a quality change that never happened.
